claims.claim: Religious diversity, the coexistence of multiple religious traditions within a society, is a pervasive social fact that scholars describe rather than evaluate; it is the descriptive starting point for most comparative study.

Globally, major religious groups are distributed unevenly: in 2015 Christians were the largest group at about 31% of the world's population, followed by Muslims (about 24%), the religiously unaffiliated (about 16%), Hindus (about 15%), and Buddhists (about 7%), with folk religions, Jews, and members of other religions making up the remainder.

The United States has been religiously diverse throughout its history, and waves of immigration, especially in the past fifty years, have brought religious traditions from around the world and reshaped American religious life, including Christianity itself.

No major religious tradition is monolithic: each contains denominations, schools, or movements, such as Judaism's Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and Reconstructionist movements; Islam's Sunni, Shi'a, and Sufi streams; and the many denominations and churches within Christianity.

In the religious marketplace framing, social scientists who apply rational choice theory describe religious life in pluralistic societies as a marketplace in which religious organizations compete for members and individuals choose among options much as they select other consumer goods.

The Pluralism Project, founded by Diana L. Eck, distinguishes diversity from pluralism: diversity is the fact of difference, while pluralism is 'the energetic engagement with diversity' — religious diversity is a given, but pluralism is an achievement, not a given.

Philosophical scholarship likewise separates descriptive religious diversity from pluralism as a family of responses to it, including exclusivist, inclusivist, and pluralist positions; the SEP entry clarifies these positions rather than endorsing one.

Religious diversity can be accompanied by documented challenges, including stereotypes and prejudice, discrimination (for example, zoning disputes over new temples, gurdwaras, and mosques), and hate crimes; both coexistence and conflict are documented outcomes of diverse societies.

The Pluralism Project describes dialogue as the language of pluralism and argues that mere diversity without real encounter and relationship can yield increasing tensions in a society; interfaith dialogue and movements are developed in the sibling topic interfaith-relations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the presence of many traditions in one society is itself beneficial or merely neutral.
positions: Diversity alone can be treated as a neutral descriptive fact about coexistence.
The Pluralism Project argues that mere diversity without encounter and relationship 'will yield increasing tensions in our societies,' so pluralism is an achievement rather than a given.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents diversity as the descriptive fact and pluralism as a form of positive engagement, attributes the distinction to Diana Eck and the Pluralism Project, and does not adjudicate between them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the religious marketplace model explains religious life adequately.
positions: Rational choice theory frames religious organizations as competing for members in a marketplace of options.
The model is one scholarly framing among several; the OpenStax overview presents it as one way social scientists have attempted to explain religious behavior, not as settled fact.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the marketplace as an attributed scholarly framing (rational choice theory) and notes it is one model, not a universal law.

sourceRecords.title: The Changing Global Religious Landscape
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A source (Pew Research Center), new record minted 2026-08-21; read the live report page. Supports the 2015 global estimates: Christians about 31% of the world's 7.3 billion people (largest group), Muslims about 24% (1.8 billion), religiously unaffiliated about 16%, Hindus about 15%, Buddhists about 7%, with folk religions, Jews, and other religions making up the remainder. Statistics reported in own words; no Pew wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Pluralism? (About) — The Pluralism Project
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A source (Harvard Pluralism Project), new record minted 2026-08-21. The live page blocks automated fetch, so it was read through a reader proxy of the live URL (same content as the page served by pluralism.org); the canonical URL is registered. Supports the attributed Eck/Pluralism Project distinction: 'pluralism is not diversity alone, but the energetic engagement with diversity'; religious diversity is a given while pluralism is an achievement; pluralism is not just tolerance, not relativism, and is based on dialogue; mere diversity without encounter and relationship can yield increasing tensions. Short attributed phrases quoted; surrounding prose synthesized.
